newsitem.title: KENYA: ICO head say Africans must focus on quality.
newsitem.headline: ICO head say Africans must focus on quality.

text.p: International Coffee Organization (ICO) Executive Director Celsius Lodder said on Friday that Africans must concentrate on research and better husbandry to improve quality, the key to their market performance.

On the sidelines of an international conference on coffee science in Nairobi, Lodder told Reuters countries must cooperate with their neighbours in research because it was more cost-effective and solved similar problems.
He said previous research problems were tackled by each country going it alone, whereas cooperating with neighbours would lessen the work in monetary terms and provide more experts.

"Kenya has to cooperate with Tanzania, Uganda, Ethiopia, Burundi and Rwanda for instance. You look at ways to enhance production for the region and ways to improve quality. That is the best way to improve the coffee profile," Lodder said.

Africa's 25 producing countries produce around 14-15 million 60-kg bags and target a level of 21-22 million bags. But civil wars, changeable weather and poor husbandry meant that target is merely a dream and in fact production might drop from present levels, according to regional crop experts.
Lodder said emphasis should be put on disease control.

"The question of quality is central to Africa's production. To improve production they have to concentrate on improving yield per acre, rather than expanding the land under coffee. That is why research is important," Lodder said.

Lodder said Uganda stood out in market liberalisation, with the government state agency ceding control of marketing but a state body retaining authority over quality control. He said that example was also followed by Kenya and Ethiopia.

In Cameroon, Lodder said quality and eventually quantity was undermined because swift liberalisation meant that the government left itself no room for control of sales and gave little in terms of support to farmers to improve crops.

"Liberalisation is very important but it must be coordinated properly. If quality is the key item, you do not want to lose it because there are traders only interested in getting their coffee at their lowest possible price," Lodder said.
"You've got to keep a form of control," he added.
Most African countries are agriculture-dependent. In Rwana, Burundi and Ethiopia, coffee is the leading commodity export.

"With the emergence of Vietnam as a major supplier, prospects elsewhere in Asia and a probable recovery in African countries, it could be expected that robusta production will grow strongly and may be in relative over-supply," Lodder said.

Lodder said Africans and other small producers had been highly protected by the ICO export quota system that collapsed in 1989. That collapse had opened Africans up to severe price volatility and their main option was to raise output and quality.

Lodder also referred to nervousness on the world market arising from information made available on production. He said too much information, some of it unreliable, got on to the market -- which unfairly influenced market trends.
